narrative:
The model estimated a 63.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged more likely than success, and because your law-school application depended on this prediction, it was denied. This is a probability, not a certainty.

The strongest influence was your third-year academic standing. Your third-year decile was 1, far below the average of about 5.79 among accepted students, and this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor. At 36 it was only slightly below the accepted-student average of 37.18, and in your case it actually leaned toward passing. The third most important factor was your first-year standing: your first-year decile was 2, well below the accepted average of 6, and it again pushed toward failure. Gender and race were not used.

To strengthen a future application, focus on explaining and remedying the academic record behind your low first- and third-year standings. Seek academic advising, consider coursework or study preparation that demonstrates readiness for law-school rigor, and ask whether you can submit context or a plan for bar-exam preparation. You may also request a human review of the decision.
